sections.b: Judges 2:11–19 sets out a pattern that the following stories repeat. Israel does "what was evil in the eyes of the LORD" and serves the Baals; the LORD's anger blazes and he sells them to an oppressor; they cry out; he raises up a rescuer; the land is quiet; the judge dies and they "behave worse than their ancestors." Othniel's story (3:7–11) uses every step and nothing else, as a model. The stories that follow keep the outline but break it more and more: Gideon's ends with an ephod and a usurper, Jephthah is chosen by the elders, and Samson never leads Israel at all.

Scholars distinguish the "major" judges, whose stories are told at length (Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson), from the "minor" judges, given a few lines each (Shamgar, Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon). Counting Deborah and including Shamgar gives twelve, one for each tribe in principle, though they come from only some of the tribes. Martin Noth argued that the minor judges came from an old list of officials who held a legal office over Israel, and that the editor gave their title to the war heroes. Others think the lists simply fill out the book's chronology.

sections.h: How long did the period last?
sections.b: Adding the years of oppression, rest and judgeship in Judges 3–16 gives about 410 years, more than the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 allows once the wilderness, Joshua, Eli, Samuel, Saul and David are added. Most readers, traditional and critical, conclude that some judges overlapped, ruling different regions at the same time; the Ammonite and Philistine oppressions in 10:7 seem to be one example. Jephthah's "three hundred years" (11:26) is often used in the debate about the date of the exodus. Critical historians place the period roughly between 1200 and 1050 BC.

common: Most readers think the judges' periods overlapped, so the book's years cannot simply be added up.
Most scholars see the repeating cycle of 2:11–19 as the work of the book's editor, laid over older stories.
uncommon: Some scholars think the twelve judges were chosen to represent the twelve tribes, a sign of careful design.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the cycle turns into a spiral
claude.body: My own observation: Othniel's story contains every step of the cycle and no detail; each later story adds detail and loses a step. Ehud has no Spirit; Deborah's story has a prophet but a reluctant warrior; Gideon has signs but ends in idolatry; Abimelech has no cry and no rescuer; Jephthah's call comes from the elders and God refuses at first; Samson never rallies Israel. I suggest the book is built so that the cycle wears away step by step until, in chapters 17–21, nothing is left but a people in which "Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (21:25). Many scholars describe the book as a downward spiral; tracing it as the loss of one element per judge is my own suggestion.

sections.b: Judges 2:6–3:6 is often called the clearest example of Deuteronomistic writing in the book. It repeats Joshua 24:28–31 to join the two books, then explains the coming stories with Deuteronomy's language: Israel "left the LORD" and served other gods, the LORD's anger blazed, he "sold them" to enemies, and he left the nations to "test" Israel (Deuteronomy 8:2; 13:3). The same frame returns in 3:7, 3:12, 4:1, 6:1, 10:6 and 13:1. Martin Noth saw this as the work of one historian writing during the exile; others, such as Wolfgang Richter, traced earlier stages, including a "book of rescuers" from the northern kingdom.

common: Most critical scholars think the cycle passages in Judges were written by the editor of the Deuteronomistic History.
uncommon: Some literary readers think the book's frame and stories are so well matched that one author composed both.

sections.h: At Bochim and under the oak (Judges 2; 6)
sections.b: The angel of the LORD speaks in the first person as God at Bochim: "I am the one who brought you up from Egypt" (2:1). At Ophrah he sits under the oak, calls Gideon a mighty fighter, and is then called simply "the LORD" (6:14, 16). He touches the offering with his staff, fire flares from the rock, and he vanishes; Gideon fears he will die for having seen him face to face (6:21–23). Deborah's song has him curse Meroz (5:23). The same figure appears to Samson's parents (chapter 13). These scenes are among the main texts in the debate over whether the angel is a messenger speaking for God or God himself appearing.

common: Many Christian readers, from Justin Martyr on, saw the angel who speaks as God as the Son before his incarnation.
uncommon: Some scholars think the word "angel" was added to older stories in which God himself appeared, to soften them.

sections.b: Judges names Baal more than any other book except Kings. Israel "served the Baals and the Ashtoreths" (2:11, 13; 10:6), the plural meaning local forms of the storm god and his consort. Gideon's own father keeps an altar of Baal with an Asherah pole beside it (6:25), and Gideon's second name, Jerubbaal, is explained as "Let Baal contend against him" (6:32). After Gideon dies, Israel makes Baal-berith, "Lord of the covenant," its god at Shechem, and that god's temple pays for Abimelech's murders (8:33; 9:4, 46). The pattern shows the appeal of a god of rain and harvest to new farmers in the hills.

common: Most scholars see Baal worship in Judges as the pull of Canaan's farming religion on Israel's new settlers.
uncommon: Some scholars think Jerubbaal was originally a Baal name honoring the god, later reinterpreted as a challenge to him.

claude.title: Claude's theory: Baal's two temples in the Gideon story
claude.body: My own reading: Gideon's story begins with Baal's altar torn down by night (6:25–28) and ends with Baal-berith's temple funding the murder of Gideon's sons and becoming their killers' fortress (9:4, 46–49). Baal, dared to "contend for himself" (6:31), seems to do so a generation later through Shechem. I suggest the narrator meant the reader to see Joash's challenge answered in an unexpected way: Baal does not strike Gideon, but Baal's people destroy his house. Then Baal's temple is itself burned. Scholars note the irony of Baal-berith's silver; reading chapter 9 as the answer to 6:31 is my own.

sections.b: Deborah is the only judge also called a prophet, and the only one shown settling cases (4:4–5). She summons Barak with the LORD's command, promises victory, and warns him that the glory will go to a woman (4:6–9). She gives the signal to attack (4:14). The woman who wins the glory is not Deborah but Jael, who kills Sisera with a tent peg (4:17–22). The rabbis counted Deborah among Israel's seven women prophets (Bavli Megillah 14a).

The Song is one of the oldest poems in the Bible. It praises the LORD who marches from Seir, calls Deborah "a mother in Israel" (5:7), praises the tribes who came and shames those who did not, tells of the stars and the Kishon fighting for Israel, blesses Jael, and ends with Sisera's mother waiting at the window. It is read in synagogues with the Song of the Sea, and scholars use its tribal list as evidence for early Israel.

common: Most scholars date the Song of Deborah earlier than the prose account in chapter 4.
uncommon: Some think Deborah's title "wife of Lappidoth" means "woman of torches," a description rather than a husband's name.

sections.b: Gideon gets more space than any judge but Samson. He is called while hiding grain in a winepress, asks for signs, pulls down his father's Baal altar, and is clothed by the Spirit (chapter 6). God shrinks his army to three hundred, sends him a dream from the enemy camp, and gives the victory with horns, jars and torches (chapter 7). Then the story darkens: he punishes Succoth and Penuel, kills the kings to avenge his brothers, refuses a crown but makes a gold ephod that Israel worships (chapter 8). His son Abimelech's bloody reign follows (chapter 9).

common: Most readers see Gideon's story as turning from faith to failure after the victory of chapter 7.
Traditional readers take Gideon's refusal of the crown (8:23) as sincere.
uncommon: Some scholars think Gideon and Jerubbaal were two separate heroes whose stories were joined.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the man who threshed, threshing men
claude.body: My own reading: Gideon's story is framed by threshing. He first appears beating out wheat in secret (6:11); he tests God on a threshing floor (6:37); and he ends his campaign by "threshing" the elders of Succoth with thorns (8:7, 16, in the Greek). I suggest the narrator uses the image to show the change in him: the farmer who threshed grain to feed his family ends by threshing his own people. Scholars note the threshing threat and the winepress; the frame from 6:11 to 8:16 is my own suggestion.

sections.b: Jephthah is a prostitute's son, driven out by his half-brothers, who gathers a band of "empty men" in Tob. When Ammon attacks, Gilead's elders recall him, and he bargains to become their head (11:1–11). He argues Israel's claim to the land in a long letter (11:12–28). The Spirit comes on him; he vows to offer whatever comes out of his door, wins, and is met by his only daughter (11:29–40). He then fights Ephraim and kills those who cannot say "Shibboleth" (12:1–6). He judges six years (12:7). Hebrews 11:32 lists him among the heroes of faith.

common: Most ancient Jewish and Christian readers believed Jephthah really sacrificed his daughter, and judged the vow sinful.
uncommon: Kimchi, Keil and Delitzsch, Hengstenberg and many evangelical commentators hold that the daughter was dedicated to lifelong virginity in God's service, not killed, reading "will be the LORD's" as dedication and 11:40 as yearly visits "to talk with" her.

claude.title: Claude's theory: Jephthah's daughter and Achsah
claude.body: My own reading: Judges begins and nearly ends its first half with a father, a vow about a daughter, and a reward for victory. Caleb promises Achsah to whoever takes Kiriath-sepher (1:12), and she rides away with a husband, land and springs. Jephthah promises "whatever comes out" to God, and his daughter goes to the hills to weep and does not come back to a husband. I suggest the two scenes are a deliberate pair, measuring how far Israel has fallen: the first daughter is given in blessing, the second is given up, whether to death or to a life with no husband. Feminist critics have compared the women of Judges as a series; pairing these two vows is my own suggestion.

sections.b: Before battle Jephthah vows that "whatever comes out" of his house to meet him will be the LORD's as a burnt offering (11:30–31). When his daughter comes out, he says he cannot go back on his word (11:35), and she agrees (11:36). The law did insist that vows be kept (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23), but it also let people vowed to God be redeemed for money (Leviticus 27:1–8) and forbade human sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31). The rabbis blamed Jephthah and Phinehas for not seeking release (Genesis Rabbah 60:3), and the story became the Bible's main warning against rash vows. Whether the vow was carried out by sacrifice or by lifelong dedication is debated (see the notes at 11:31 and 11:39).

The first half of Judges is full of holy-war language: the LORD "put the Canaanites and the Perizzites in their power" (1:4), Zephath is put under the ban and renamed Hormah (1:17), the LORD "marched out ahead" of Barak and threw Sisera into panic (4:14–15), the stars fought from heaven (5:20), and the LORD turned Midian's swords on each other (7:22). God shrinks Gideon's army so Israel cannot boast (7:2), and the fearful are sent home (7:3) as Deuteronomy 20:8 commands. Yet the book also tells of failure: the tribes do not drive out the Canaanites (1:27–36), and the LORD will no longer drive them out (2:21).

After Midian's defeat the Israelites offer Gideon a dynasty, and he refuses: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. The LORD will rule over you" (8:23). His son Abimelech, whose name means "my father is king," has himself made king at Shechem by killing his seventy brothers (9:1–6). Jotham's fable of the trees who anoint a thornbush mocks the choice (9:7–15), and Abimelech's three years end in civil war and a millstone (9:22–57). Together these chapters are the Bible's first sustained reflection on kingship, and they shape Samuel's warning in 1 Samuel 8.

common: Many scholars read Jotham's fable as one of the strongest anti-monarchic texts in the Bible.
uncommon: Some think the fable criticizes only a king chosen wrongly, not kingship itself, since the book later longs for a king.

sections.b: The Spirit of the LORD comes on Othniel and he judges Israel (3:10). The Spirit "put Gideon on like clothing" (6:34), a phrase used again only of Amasai and Zechariah the priest (1 Chronicles 12:18; 2 Chronicles 24:20). The Spirit comes on Jephthah before he makes his vow (11:29). In each case the Spirit gives power to lead in war, not wisdom or goodness: Gideon still asks for signs, and Jephthah still makes his fatal vow.

The Philistines first appear in Judges as one of the nations left to test Israel: "the five rulers of the Philistines" (3:3). Shamgar kills six hundred of them with an ox goad (3:31). In 10:7 the LORD sells Israel to the Philistines and the Ammonites at once, setting up both Jephthah's story in the east and Samson's in the west. The Hebrew of 1:18 says Judah took three Philistine cities, while the Greek says it did not.

For seven years Midian, with Amalek and "the people of the East," invaded at harvest with tents, flocks and camels coming "as thick as a swarm of locusts" (6:3–5). Their defeat by Gideon became proverbial: Isaiah speaks of "the day of Midian" (Isaiah 9:4) and the blow "at Oreb's Rock" (Isaiah 10:26), and Psalm 83:11 prays that God treat his enemies as he did Oreb and Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna. The camel raids are among the earliest in the Bible to describe camels used in war.

Eglon king of Moab, with Ammon and Amalek, takes the City of Palms and makes Israel pay tribute for eighteen years, until Ehud kills him in his private room (3:12–30). Jephthah's letter to Ammon recalls that Israel went around Moab and never took its land, and that Balak of Moab never went to war with Israel (11:15–18, 25). The rabbis said Ruth the Moabite descended from Eglon.

Gideon's concubine lives in Shechem, and their son Abimelech wins the town's lords by appealing to kinship (8:31; 9:1–3). Shechem makes him king "by the oak of the pillar," where Joshua had set up a stone of witness (9:6; Joshua 24:26). Jotham shouts his fable from Mount Gerizim above the town (9:7). After three years Shechem revolts under Gaal, appealing to "the men of Hamor" (9:28; Genesis 34), and Abimelech destroys it and burns its tower temple of El-berith (9:45–49). Excavations at Tell Balata show a destruction of the city in the twelfth century BC and a massive fortress temple. The temple's date is disputed: the excavators placed its great phase in the Middle Bronze Age, too early for Abimelech, while Lawrence Stager re-dated its use into Iron Age I.

Judges 1:8 says the people of Judah took Jerusalem and burned it, but 1:21 says the Benjaminites did not drive out the Jebusites, who lived on there "until today." Joshua 15:63 tells the same about Judah. Most readers think Judah raided the city without holding it; David finally took the stronghold (2 Samuel 5:6–9). Adoni-bezek dies there (1:7).

The house of Joseph takes Bethel, once called Luz, after a man shows them the way in and is spared with his family; he goes off and builds a new Luz among the Hittites (1:22–26). The story reverses Rahab's: here the Canaanite is spared for betraying his town, but does not join Israel. Bochim, where Israel weeps (2:1–5), may have been near Bethel, as the Greek suggests, and Deborah judges between Ramah and Bethel (4:5).

Judges repeats Joshua's account of Caleb's offer of his daughter Achsah to whoever takes Kiriath-sepher, Othniel's victory, and Achsah's request for springs (1:11–15; Joshua 15:15–19). It notes that Hebron was given to Caleb "as Moses had said" (1:20). Othniel, Caleb's younger brother (or nephew; see 1:13), becomes the first judge (3:9–11), linking the faithful generation of the conquest with the period of the judges.

"The family of the Kenite who was Moses' father-in-law" goes up with Judah and settle near Arad (1:16). Heber the Kenite, descended from Hobab, "Moses' father-in-law," has moved north and is at peace with Jabin (4:11, 17). His wife Jael kills Sisera (4:21). The family of Moses' in-laws thus plays a part in Israel's story long after the wilderness. Judges calls the father-in-law Hobab, where Exodus calls him Jethro or Reuel.

Gideon's ephod is made like the golden calf: the leader asks for the people's gold earrings, the people give them, the leader makes an object, and Israel worships it (8:24–27; Exodus 32:2–4). Both follow a great rescue. Judges says the ephod "became a trap for Gideon and his house" (8:27). Later, Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan repeat the sin on a larger scale (1 Kings 12:28–30).

Jephthah tells the Ammonite king that Israel has lived in Heshbon and the Arnon towns "for three hundred years" (11:26). Supporters of an exodus around 1446 BC take this as support for their date, since three centuries before Jephthah reaches back into the fifteenth century. Supporters of a thirteenth-century exodus reply that Jephthah was making a diplomatic point in round numbers, or adding up the book's overlapping periods.

sections.h: The two Greek texts of Judges
sections.b: Judges is one of the books where the Greek Old Testament differs most within itself. Alfred Rahlfs printed two complete texts on facing pages: the A text, close to Codex Alexandrinus, and the B text, close to Codex Vaticanus. They differ in vocabulary and sometimes in meaning, as at 5:2 ("when leaders took the lead" or "a revelation was revealed"). The Greek also has readings that differ from the Hebrew, such as 1:18 (Judah did not take Gaza) and an added line at 4:8. A Dead Sea Scroll fragment, 4QJudg-a, lacks 6:7–10, which may show an earlier form of the book.

Jephthah's daughter is called his "one and only child" (11:34), echoing God's words to Abraham about Isaac (Genesis 22:2). Both stories have a father, a child and a burnt offering, but in Judges there is no command from God, no ram, and no voice from heaven. Jewish and Christian readers since antiquity have set the two side by side. Pseudo-Philo has God say that he will let Jephthah's daughter die because of his rash vow, while honoring her as wiser than her father.

Jephthah's vow (11:31) is set among peoples who did practice child sacrifice in crisis. The king of Moab offered his firstborn on the wall when losing a war (2 Kings 3:27), and the law forbids Israel to burn children as the nations did (Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10). Many scholars think the story assumes this background, whether or not Jephthah understood his vow that way.

When the angel vanishes, Gideon cries out, "Oh no, Lord GOD! ... Now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!" (6:22). The LORD assures him he will not die (6:23). The scene draws on the belief that no one can see God and live (Exodus 33:20), which Jacob (Genesis 32:30) and later Manoah (13:22) also voice.

Gideon is sent to overhear a Midianite soldier telling a dream: a round loaf of barley bread rolls into the camp and flattens a tent. His friend explains it as "the sword of Gideon" (7:13–14). As with Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar, God speaks through the dreams of outsiders; here the dream is meant as much for the listener as for the dreamer.

Judges 1 reports tribe by tribe: Judah and Simeon succeed, Benjamin, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali and Dan fail to drive out the Canaanites. The Song of Deborah praises the tribes that came and shames those that stayed home, and does not name Judah or Simeon (5:14–18). Ephraim twice resents being left out of victory (8:1–3; 12:1–6), and the second time Gilead kills forty-two thousand of them.

Gideon has "many wives" and seventy sons, plus a concubine in Shechem (8:30–31), the kind of household Deuteronomy forbids to a king (Deuteronomy 17:17). The concubine's son Abimelech kills the seventy (9:5), the first of many Bible stories in which rivalry among the sons of different mothers ends in blood. Jephthah, son of a prostitute, is driven out by his father's wife's sons (11:1–2).

sections.h: "A womb or two for every man" (Judges 5)
sections.b: The Song of Deborah imagines Sisera's mother consoling herself that the soldiers are sharing out plunder: "A womb or two for every man" (5:30). The crude word shows how captured women were seen as spoils. The poem sets this beside Jael's killing of Sisera in language that some scholars read as a reversal of rape (5:27). These lines begin the book's dark thread of violence against women.

Judges 9 contains no miracle and no rescue. God acts only by sending a spirit of discord (9:23) and, at the end, by repaying Abimelech and Shechem for their crimes (9:56–57). Readers have long used the chapter as an example of providence working through human choices: the murderers fall out, a stone for a stone, and Jotham's curse comes true.

Israel's confession in 10:10–16 is the fullest in Judges. God at first refuses, telling them to cry to the gods they chose; they confess again, put away the foreign gods, and serve the LORD. Readers debate whether God's last word, that he "had had enough of Israel's misery," means pity or weariness.

Jephthah says to the Ammonite king, "Whatever your god Chemosh gives you to possess, you take possession of" (11:24). Readers ask whether this concedes that other gods are real. Many think Jephthah argues on his opponent's terms; others see an early stage of Israel's faith in which each nation had its god but Israel owed loyalty to the LORD alone.
